extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans, and researchers interested in Saturday Night Live and live sketch-comedy production
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, production practices, and commercial considerations observed in the creation, performance, and spin-offs of Saturday Night Live — covering live performance norms, weekly production rhythms, guest-host roles, adaptations to crises, commercial tie-ins, film spin-offs, music licensing, and documentary access. Useful for people studying or attempting to produce SNL-style live sketch television or related tie-in projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live performance policy (no lip-sync)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted guidance/citation: "Michaels: Lip-Sync An 'SNL' No-No" — SNL has an established expectation against lip-syncing performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a production norm (cited from an interview/report). Implication: musical and performance acts are expected to perform live; lip-syncing is considered against show policy. (See citations: Leung, Rebecca (February 11, 2009).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Intense weekly writing and production schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: From a 60 Minutes report: "the intense writing frenzy that goes on during the week leading up to a show, with crowded meetings and long hours."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the standard weekly workflow and expectation: high-pressure, iterative meetings and long hours culminate in producing the live show each week. Used to explain difficulty of getting sketches on-air and the demands faced by cast and writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest host involvement in sketch development
rubrics_metrics.description: "The report particularly noted the involvement of the guest host(s) in developing and selecting the sketches in which they will appear."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guideline: guest hosts are not just performers but participate actively in creating and choosing material for their appearances. Producers and writers coordinate with hosts during the week to shape sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production adaptation in response to public-health or extraordinary events
rubrics_metrics.description: Documented actions: "SNL to Suspend Production Due to the Coronavirus" and "SNL Drops Live Audience and Musical Guest Charli XCX Due to COVID Spike."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows may alter format (suspend production, drop live audience, remove musical guests) in response to health risks or other emergencies. These are accepted production adjustments and part of the show's contingency practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting live coast-to-coast (airing live in all time zones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted milestone: "SNL to Air Live in All Time Zones for First Time Ever" — efforts have been made to broadcast the show live across time zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects a production/airing policy decision to present the program live across the country; implications include synchronization of live elements and managing time-zone logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial tie‑ins and character-based advertising (with reputational risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Over the years popular characters from the show have appeared in ad campaigns for an assortment of products." The article lists many examples (State Farm, Subway, Acura, BMW, Pepsi, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples show that character-based commercials are common revenue/brand collaborations but carry reputational and PR risk: campaigns have been pulled (e.g., 'It's Pat' film pulled after poor reception), ads withdrawn in response to actors' off-screen statements or controversy (Rob Schneider example), or companies/retailers declining products after boycotts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film spin-off success measured by commercial and critical reception
rubrics_metrics.description: "SNL has made several efforts to develop some of the more popular sketches into feature-length films, with varying degrees of commercial and critical success." (Examples: The Blues Brothers, Wayne's World vs. It's Pat, Stuart Saves His Family.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of sketch-to-film adaptations relies on box-office revenue, budget comparisons, and critical reception. The article's film table (budgets and box office) is used as the primary metric to judge success or failure of spin-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music releases and licensing requirements for SNL-developed songs
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: The Lonely Island albums were "released by Universal Republic Records, which was provided with a license to the SNL songs by NBC and Broadway Video."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When releasing music originating on the show, third parties require licensing from NBC/Broadway Video. Legal/rights clearance is a necessary production and distribution criterion for SNL-derived music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary and behind‑the‑scenes productions require access to contributors and rare footage
rubrics_metrics.description: Books and documentaries such as Live From New York and James Franco's 94-minute documentary consist of interviews and backstage access; Franco's project expanded after Lorne Michaels "granted Franco access to the process."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing authoritative behind-the-scenes histories or documentaries depends on access to cast, writers, execs, and archival footage; interview-based oral histories are a recognized method for documenting backstage production and the difficulties of mounting a weekly live show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product tie‑ins can provoke public backlash and boycotts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ben & Jerry's limited-edition ice cream 'Schweddy Balls' (inspired by an SNL sketch) "was subject to criticism and boycotts by One Million Moms ... some retail chains chose not to sell the flavor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that branding decisions tied to SNL content may trigger consumer or advocacy group backlash; manufacturers and retailers may choose not to participate or to withdraw products, so PR risk assessments are a production/marketing criterion.
